scenes.title: Foundation: iterated integration and regions
scenes.objective: Recall single integrals and area elements.

ask.q: What does a double integral ∬ᴿf(x,y)dA accumulate?
ask.nudge: It accumulates a scalar quantity over a two-dimensional region.

body: A double integral extends definite integration to a region in the plane. It can represent area, volume under a surface, mass from a density or total probability.
An iterated integral evaluates the same accumulation one variable at a time. The limits must describe the region correctly, and a change of variables introduces a Jacobian factor.

items.ask: What is Fubini's theorem used for?
items.recall: It allows a double integral to be evaluated as an iterated integral under suitable integrability conditions.
refresh: For a continuous function on a rectangle, integrate with respect to one variable and then the other. The order may be reversed, with limits adjusted to describe the same region.
For more general regions, describe the bounds carefully. If the region is not rectangular, the inner limits often depend on the outer variable.

items.recall: The determinant of the matrix of first partial derivatives of the transformation.
refresh: For x=x(u,v), y=y(u,v), the Jacobian is ∂(x,y)/∂(u,v)=xᵤyᵥ−xᵥyᵤ. It measures local area scaling under the transformation.
In a change of variables, dA=|J|dudv. The absolute value is essential because area is non-negative even if the transformation reverses orientation.

items.ask: What is the area element in polar coordinates?
refresh: The transformation x=r cosθ, y=r sinθ has Jacobian r. Therefore dxdy becomes r dr dθ, not simply dr dθ.
The extra factor r accounts for the fact that a small angular sector has arc length r dθ. Forgetting r is one of the most common errors in polar integration.

scenes.title: A double integral is accumulated area or volume
scenes.objective: Interpret the geometry of multiple integration.

ask.q: Why does the polar area element contain r?
ask.nudge: The angular width corresponds to an arc of length r dθ.

body: A double integral over a region sums contributions from tiny area pieces. If f=1, the result is the area of the region. If f is a height, it gives volume under the surface.
In polar coordinates, tiny sectors widen as r increases. The Jacobian r corrects the area of each transformed rectangle in (r,θ)-space.

scenes.title: Fubini's theorem on rectangles
scenes.objective: Evaluate double integrals as iterated integrals.

ask.q: For continuous f on [a,b]×[c,d], can the order of integration be reversed?
ask.nudge: Yes, under the rectangle and continuity conditions.

blocks.body: Integrate the inner variable first, treating the outer variable as a constant. Then integrate the resulting expression over the outer interval.
Both orders give the same value when the hypotheses hold, but one may produce simpler inner limits or algebra. Choose the order that best matches the region and integrand.

scenario.teaser: A density is accumulated over a rectangular plate.
scenario.title: Mass from a two-dimensional density
body: Suppose a thin plate occupies a rectangle R and has density ρ(x,y). Its total mass is ∬ᴿρ(x,y)dA.
For a rectangular region, Fubini's theorem evaluates the mass as an iterated integral. The inner integral accumulates along one coordinate and the outer integral accumulates across the other.
The units provide a check: density per unit area multiplied by area gives mass. If the density is constant, the result reduces to density times the rectangle's area.

scenes.title: Non-rectangular regions and changing order
scenes.objective: Set limits from the geometry of a region.

ask.q: For 0≤x≤1 and 0≤y≤x, what is the outer x-range?
ask.nudge: x runs from zero to one.

blocks.body: A region may be written a≤x≤b and g₁(x)≤y≤g₂(x). Then integrate y first with x-dependent limits.
Alternatively c≤y≤d and h₁(y)≤x≤h₂(y). Then integrate x first with y-dependent limits.
Sketch the region, identify its left/right and lower/upper boundaries, then choose an order. Reversing order changes the bounds, not the region or integral value.

scenes.objective: Transform an integral into simpler coordinates.

blocks.body: x=r cosθ, y=r sinθ; the Jacobian is r, so dA=r dr dθ.
A change of variables requires transforming the integrand, the region and the area element. All three must be updated consistently.

scenes.title: Triple integrals accumulate volume and mass
scenes.objective: Extend the same idea to three dimensions.

ask.nudge: It is the volume of the region V.

body: A triple integral accumulates a scalar field over a three-dimensional region. With integrand one, it gives volume; with a density, it gives mass.
For a rectangular box, use three nested integrals. For cylindrical or spherical symmetry, coordinate changes can simplify the region, but their Jacobians must be included.

scenario.teaser: A density varies throughout a three-dimensional solid.
scenario.title: Mass of a solid from a volume density
body: If a solid V has density ρ(x,y,z), its total mass is ∭_Vρ(x,y,z)dV. A constant density gives mass equal to density times volume.

For a rectangular box, Fubini evaluates the triple integral as three nested one-dimensional integrals. For cylindrical symmetry, cylindrical coordinates may simplify the limits and the volume element.
The same rule applies: transform the region and include the Jacobian. In cylindrical coordinates dV=r dr dθ dz; omitting r gives an incorrect volume and mass.

scenes.title: Trap check: six statements
scenes.intro: Judge each statement true or false.

items.claim: Fubini permits order reversal under suitable integrability conditions.
items.why: The iterated integrals agree under the theorem's hypotheses.

items.claim: The polar area element is dr dθ.
items.why: The Jacobian factor r is required.

items.claim: The Jacobian enters as an absolute value.
Changing variables requires transforming the region.
items.why: The new bounds must describe the same region.

items.claim: A double integral of one gives the area of the region.
items.why: It accumulates unit density over the region.

items.claim: A triple integral of one gives surface area.
items.why: It gives volume; surface area is a two-dimensional measure.

scenes.title: Final multiple-integration checklist
body: 1. Draw or describe the region before choosing integration limits.
2. Use Fubini to evaluate as nested one-dimensional integrals when conditions hold.
3. For non-rectangular regions, make inner limits depend on the outer variable.
4. Change of variables: transform integrand, region and area element.
5. Polar coordinates: x=r cosθ, y=r sinθ and dA=r dr dθ.
6. Triple integral of one gives volume; density gives mass.
7. Cylindrical coordinates use dV=r dr dθ dz.
